blocks.text: Ask for a drink almost anywhere in Turkey and you'll be offered *çay*: in offices and shops, at the bank, on a ferry, in a friend's living room. Turkey drinks more tea per person than any other country, more than 3 kg of leaves a year according to the Turkish Statistical Institute, or roughly four glasses a day for every man, woman and child.

It wasn't always so. In Ottoman times the drink of conversation was coffee. After the First World War the empire lost Yemen, where its coffee grew, and coffee became expensive and sometimes scarce. The young Republic decided to grow tea at home, on the mild and rainy eastern Black Sea coast. A law of February 1924 encouraged tea, hazelnuts and citrus around Rize, with seedlings brought from Batumi, just across the Georgian border, but real plantations only came after 1937, when seed arrived in bulk, and a Tea Law in 1940. The first tea factory opened in Rize in 1947.

Today the green terraces of Rize and its neighbouring provinces grow nearly all Turkish tea, much of it bought and processed by the state company ÇAYKUR. Most of it is drunk at home; only a small share is exported.

Tea is brewed in a *çaydanlık*, a double teapot. Water boils in the large lower pot, and the leaves steep in the small upper one, the *demlik*. Each glass gets some of the strong brew from the top and is topped up with hot water from below, so everyone can have it *koyu* (dark, strong) or *açık* (light). It is drunk without milk, often with a cube or two of sugar, from a small tulip-shaped glass called *ince belli*, slim-waisted, which you hold by the rim because the tea is very hot.

Outdoors, the *çay bahçesi* (tea garden) is a café under the trees where friends and families sit for hours, glass after glass, while a waiter with a tray goes from table to table. Nobody hurries you.

blocks.title: Açık and koyu
blocks.text: *Açık* also means **open**, as you saw in [unit 4](a1-u04). With tea, *açık* is weak and *koyu* strong: *Açık bir çay, lütfen* (A weak tea, please).
